The Cloudy squeaker (Synodontis nebulosus) is a comparatively small-bodied mormyrid from the rivers of West Africa. Examination of museum series and field-caught specimens indicates that adults attain a maximum total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a modest size that places this species among the smaller members of its genus. At the onset of gonadal development, individuals typically measure around 8 centimeters [Lp = around 8 centimeters] in total length, which marks the transition from the juvenile to the sub-adult growth phase. This length at puberty is consistent with the general size-structure observed in congeneric species from similar floodplain habitats, where early maturation is thought to be an adaptation to seasonal environments with high adult mortality. The allometric relationship between body length and mass in this species follows a power function, from which we estimate that a female at the pubertal length of 8 centimeters would carry a corresponding wet weight of approximately 6.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.9 grams], reflecting the moderate energetic investment in body tissues required before the onset of reproduction.

Reproductive output in Synodontis nebulosus has been assessed indirectly through fecundity estimates derived from related species. Based on the measured fecundity of Synodontis schall scaled for body size, a mature female at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] could achieve a total annual output of roughly 47 eggs per year, which translates to a daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.13 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.13 eggs per day]. This annual output is realized through a single protracted spawning event each season, yielding a reproductive frequency of 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year]. These spawning events occur during the rising flood stage when water temperatures are near 25 °C, a thermal regime that synchronizes gamete release with peak zooplankton availability for the developing larvae. The combination of a modest clutch size but sustained single annual bout classifies this species as a low-fecundity strategist relative to other Synodontis species that produce multiple broods per season.

The early life stages of the Cloudy squeaker are characterized by a relatively short incubation period. Eggs deposited at a stable water temperature of 25 °C hatch after approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a developmental rate that is typical for the genus given the small diameter of the fertilized ovum at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight of roughly 0.00052 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of one millimeter recorded in Synodontis clarias. This minimal initial mass reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the prolarva, necessitating a rapid transition to exogenous feeding. The brief egg phase and the small size at hatching are consistent with life-history strategies observed in other floodplain-spawning mormyrids, where high water temperatures accelerate embryonic development at the cost of producing altricial larvae that must quickly locate suitable planktonic prey upon yolk-sac resorption.

Adult body size in Synodontis nebulosus follows a predictable growth trajectory, with the maximum recorded wet weight in mature individuals reaching 42.7 grams [Wwi = 42.7 grams]. This asymptotic mass, estimated from the length-weight relationship derived for the genus, corresponds to the 15 centimeter ultimate total length observed in the largest field-caught specimens. The mass at birth is approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], meaning that a single female can produce offspring that collectively gain mass by several orders of magnitude over development. Under the same thermal conditions used for the incubation studies, namely a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], captive individuals have been documented to survive for a maximum of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days], which is equivalent to roughly eight years. This longevity estimate, based on records for the closely related Synodontis clarias, suggests that the Cloudy squeaker follows a relatively slow-paced life history for a fish of its size, with a substantial adult phase following rapid early growth.

Several lines of evidence indicate that the species' life span is extended relative to many other small-bodied floodplain fishes. Field studies in the Niger Basin have recovered recaptured individuals of Synodontis nebulosus that were at least eight years [am = eight years] old, a duration aligning well with the maximum longevity of 2,920 days inferred from captive observations at 2 at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]5 °C. The wet weight at maturity of 6.9 grams [Wwp = 6.9 grams] is reached relatively early in the growth cycle, consistent with the size threshold required for initial gonadal development. In contrast, the ultimate adult wet weight of 42.7 grams [Wwi = 42.7 grams] is attained only after several additional years of growth, a pattern that aligns with the slow, decelerated growth trajectory observed among mormyrids that partition energy reserves into successive spawning events rather than a single, concentrated reproductive episode. The difference of approximately seven centimeters between the total length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] and the ultimate adult length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] suggests that a substantial portion of the lifespan is spent in the sexually mature but still-growing phase, a common pattern among iteroparous floodplain fishes that experience variable interannual recruitment success.
